papers.title: Configurationally Locked Ridaifen-B Analogs as Potent Ebola Virus Entry Inhibitors.
papers.abstract: In the face of emerging outbreaks, high mortality rates, and limited treatment options, Ebola virus (EBOV) disease poses a global public health threat, underscoring the need for effective therapies. The unique and critical role that EBOV glycoprotein (GP) plays in the viral life cycle makes it an attractive target for antiviral drug discovery. In this study, we report on the design, synthesis, and evaluation of a series of cyclized ridaifen-B-based inhibitors with enhanced antiviral activity and selectivity against EBOV. Several compounds exhibited nanomolar potency inhibiting EBOV-GP-mediated entry and submicromolar potency against Marburg virus entry. Site-directed mutagenesis indicated inhibitor binding at the EBOV GP1/GP2 fusion loop. The compounds displayed favorable in vitro pharmacokinetic parameters, which encouraged testing the in vivo rapid PK for hit compound 41. papers.full_text: nature immunology https://doi.org/10.1038/s41590-026-02623-2 Comment Accelerating the research response to the Bundibugyo virus emergency Mariah P. Csolle, Bronwyn A. Bailey, Yuna Chung, Tsharni R. Zazryn, Tari Turner, David S. Khoury & Miles P. Davenport In the context of a Public Health Emergency of International Concern, such as the Bundibugyo virus outbreak, the research community requires rapid access to information to guide an effective response. Evidence mapping brings together the available knowledge in a field into a single, organized resource, enabling researchers to rapidly identify priorities, gaps and opportunities for action. Immunology and microbiology research is crucial for combatting emerging infectious diseases. This was demonstrated during the COVID-19 pandemic when multiple vaccines, monoclonal antibody treatments and diagnostics were rapidly developed. The recent World Health Organization declaration of the Bundibugyo virus (BDBV) out- break in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo as a Public Health Emer- gency of International Concern (PHEIC) signals the need for researchers to once again respond dynamically to address a major health crisis. A challenge for immunologists in pivoting their research to a new area is knowing what has already been studied, and what the priorities are. Determining this requires investigators to have an overview of the lit- erature in the new field and to be confident that they have not missed a crucial study that might affect the direction or usefulness of their research. For individual investigators, this first step of gaining an over- view of the literature in a new field can require a substantial investment of time and act as a barrier to entry. But what if all the relevant literature on the topic had already been assembled and categorized? Evidence mapping aims to provide exactly that resource, enabling researchers to quickly find all the published research that is relevant to their work. Evidence mapping of filovirus research Evidence mapping is a systematic process for identifying relevant pub- lications in a specific area and categorizing them according to the evi- dence they provide (Fig. 1). The identified literature is then displayed as a two-dimensional map categorized according to population (for example, human, non-human primate (NHP), mouse), intervention (for example, vaccination, infection, treatment) and the outcomes measured (for example, antibody response, T cell response, outcome of infection). In contrast to traditional narrative literature reviews, an evidence map is specifically designed to provide a comprehensive and unbiased assembly of the available research, enabling researchers to conduct their own downstream analyses. The screening and mapping are performed independently by two reviewers to help ensure consist- ency, and the resulting maps can be disseminated as a resource for the wider research community. Maps can also be made ‘living’ by regular updates to keep them current. In 2024, the Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations (CEPI) identified the benefits of assembling the existing evidence on immunity and vaccination for their priority pathogens and providing this as an open resource for the health and medical communities. CEPI commissioned the development of evidence maps for three filoviruses, Marburg virus (MARV), Sudan virus (SUDV) and Ebola virus (EBOV), Check for updates Step 1: Systematically search databases Step 2: Screen title and abstracts Step 3: Screen full text and tag Step 4: Evidence map Search strategy: virus and (vaccine or model/assay) Potentially relevant → progress to full text BDBV vaccine efficacy Vaccination Mice Irrelevant: exclude BDBV vaccination in NHP Natural history of BDBV NHP Vaccine ELISA Human Infection Survival Categorize relevant articles Searchable map of all relevant studies Mouse studies Vaccine Infection outcomes Survival Viral load Treatment Infection challenge Fig. 1 | Mapping the immunological evidence for BDBV. Mapping involves systematically searching to identify the relevant literature, title and abstract screening to exclude irrelevant publications, and then reviewing the full texts to identify and categorize the relevant articles according to population, intervention and outcome reported. The final map enables rapid identification of all the available literature on a topic. ELISA, enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay. nature immunology Comment which were first produced in early 2025 and updated in September 2025. When the BDBV PHEIC was declared on 17 May 2026, the map- ping team rapidly assembled to make a map of the available evidence on BDBV vaccination and immunity. The resulting map was posted online on 21 May 2026 and updated on 22 July 2026 (available at https:// livingevidence.org.au/research-initiatives/about-feeva/evidence- maps/), and a preprint1 of the methods was published on 24 May 2026. Rapid production of an evidence map for BDBV was possible because of the established method for mapping filoviruses2 and the fact that only a small number of studies on BDBV immunity were available. A total of 49 publications were included on the original map (with an additional eight included in subsequent updates). By contrast, the equivalent maps for EBOV, MARV and SUDV include 857, 198 and 147 publications, respectively. Immunological findings for BDBV Immunity to filoviruses is thought to be largely mediated through antibodies to the surface glycoprotein. Two vaccines for EBOV have been approved, both based on the EBOV glycoprotein. Unfortunately, early evidence indicates limited cross-reactivity between the EBOV and BDBV glycoproteins, and it remains unclear whether EBOV vaccines will be effective against BDBV3. A number of animal studies have shown that BDBV glycoprotein-based vaccines and monoclonal antibodies to the BDBV glycoprotein can protect from severe infection4,5. Animal models of vaccination and infection were central to the approval of the Zabdeno/Mvabea vaccine for EBOV. These studies demonstrated that vaccine-induced antibody levels were associated with protection in a NHP model of EBOV infection6. By comparing the protective antibody levels in NHPs and the antibody levels induced after human vaccination, the investigators predicted that Zabdeno/Mvabea would be protective against EBOV infection in humans. Could a similar immunobridging approach be used in BDBV? Numerous animal models have been used for BDBV (including NHPs, mice, ferrets, pigs). However, only four stud- ies have looked at the association between vaccine-induced antibody levels and protection from infection in a cynomolgus macaque model of BDBV infection. Two studies analyzed prophylactic vaccination, with one study showing an association between antibody levels and protection7 but another study showing no association8. Similarly, two studies analyzed vaccination around the time of infection. While one study of vaccination 3 or 7 days before infection showed an associa- tion between antibody levels and viral levels (in a non-peer-reviewed preprint9), another study of post-exposure prophylaxis was dif- ficult to interpret because of the dynamic nature of early immune responses to vaccination and infection4. Further work on correlates of protection from BDBV infection in NHPs is clearly needed to support potential immunobridging. Understanding the immune response to natural BDBV infection — and whether natural immunity confers immunity to reinfection — could also inform the immune responses required for protection. However, there are only 10 studies of immune responses in survivors of BDBV (none of which measured T cell responses). In the case of EBOV, previous infection is thought to confer at least short-term immunity to reinfection (although cases of viral recrudescence have been reported; reviewed in ref. 10). However, it is not clear whether BDBV infection confers subsequent immunity to BDBV reinfection. Studies of the phenotype and durability of immune responses in survivors of BDBV infection — and whether or which of these responses confer protection from reinfection — are an important priority. Key to this is the develop- ment and dissemination of validated immunoassays for BDBV, which is critical to enable comparison of immune responses across natural history and vaccination studies, and to compare responses between animal models and human infection. Challenges and future directions While analysis of the current immunological literature on BDBV (through the evidence map) highlights the need for further charac- terization of immunity to BDBV, the challenges of performing such research should not be underestimated. The outbreak itself is occur- ring in a resource-limited setting affected by conflict. BDBV is highly pathogenic, meaning it must usually be handled in biosafety level 4 facilities, greatly reducing the number of laboratories that can perform such studies. However, the challenge of BDBV research also highlights the importance of using robust, validated and, ideally, standardized assays in those studies that are performed. Further, these studies should focus on the key gaps in BDBV knowledge that are most important for the public health response and for the development of vaccines and therapeutics. Comparison with the work on EBOV, SUDV and MARV gives a useful perspective on what is possible. Evidence mapping pro- vides a novel approach to support the research community, accelerat- ing research to resolve the current BDBV outbreak and providing a key tool to support research on future health threats. analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者将证据映射解释为一种变革性工具,通过提供集中、有组织的资源,加速对新出现的传染病 暴发 的研究反应。他们强调了其新颖之处,即对 丝状病毒 研究进行系统分类,以指导突发公共卫生事件期间采取行动的优先事项和机会。

At a glance CDC established its office in Guinea in 2015 to strengthen national public health systems and enhance the country’s capacity to prevent, detect, and respond to infectious disease threats. Working in close partnership with the Ministry of Health (MOH), the National Agency for Health Security (ANSS), and other national and international partners, CDC Guinea supports efforts to build resilient surveillance systems, expand the skilled public health workforce, and advance global health security and epidemic preparedness across all levels of the health system. CDC’s work aims to protect the health of Americans and support public health around the world. Key accomplishments CDC Guinea works to stop outbreaks at their source. Strengthened infectious disease surveillance and outbreak response by supporting the ANSS to implement the 7-1-7 approach and enhance real-time data reporting through the District Health Information System (DHIS2) Expanded workforce capacity through the Field Epidemiology Training Program, training epidemiologists on the One Health approach for professionals from the human, animal, and environmental health sectors Improved laboratory systems by providing technical assistance for biosafety, diagnostic capacity, and quality assurance through the Global Laboratory Leadership Program and national specimen referral policy implementation Strengthened immunization and disease control efforts through the Expanded Program on Immunization, supporting measles, polio, meningitis, and yellow fever surveillance and vaccination campaigns Enhanced national emergency preparedness and response capacity through the Public Health Emergency Management program, strengthening Public Health Emergency Operations Centers and Rapid Intervention Teams across all 38 districts Advanced cross-sectoral collaboration integrating human, animal, and environmental surveillance systems to prevent and control zoonotic diseases such as rabies and anthrax Global health security CDC’s global health security work in Guinea focuses on strengthening the country’s capacity to prevent, detect, and respond to infectious disease threats. In partnership with the MOH and other national and international partners. CDC Guinea supports integrated surveillance systems, laboratory networks, workforce development, emergency management, and immunization programs that collectively enhance national and global health security. Health systems strengthening CDC provides technical and financial support to strengthen Guinea’s Integrated Disease Surveillance and Response system. This includes integrating Event-Based Surveillance into the District Health Information System (DHIS2) and EMPRES-i platforms, improving early warning and rapid response capabilities. Through collaboration with ANSS, CDC has helped operationalize a multi-tiered surveillance structure with Rapid Response Teams (EPARE and ERARE) and Emergency Operations Centers across all levels. These efforts improve data reporting, analysis, and decision-making through the National Health Information System. Workforce development Since 2016, CDC has supported Guinea’s Field Epidemiology Training Program (FETP), which builds critical workforce capacity for outbreak investigation and disease surveillance. To date, more than 400 public health professionals have graduated across the frontline, intermediate, and advanced levels. Over 80% remain active in country, applying their skills in managing public health emergencies such as Ebola, Marburg virus disease, COVID-19, yellow fever, and polio. The FETP follows a learning-through-service model that emphasizes field practice, mentorship, and One Health collaboration across human, animal, and environmental health sectors. Laboratory systems strengthening CDC collaborates with the National Institute of Public Health and National Directorate of Laboratories to strengthen Guinea’s diagnostic capacity. Key achievements include integrating LabBook with DHIS2 for real-time laboratory data management, launching a Global Laboratory Leadership Program in Guinea, and enhancing testing capacity for Ebola, monkeypox, COVID-19, meningitis, rotavirus, influenza, and other priority diseases. These initiatives have improved biosafety/biosecurity, quality assurance, and coordination between national and regional laboratories. Emergency management CDC helped establish Guinea’s first Public Health Emergency Operations Center, now operational in all 38 districts. CDC continues to strengthen emergency preparedness through the Public Health Emergency Management program. This collaboration supports training, simulation exercises, with standardized operating procedures to ensure coordinated response to health emergencies. Immunization CDC supports Guinea’s Expanded Program on Immunization to increase vaccine coverage and strengthen surveillance for measles, polio, yellow fever, and Meningitis A. Through the deployment of FETP-trained epidemiologists and STOP Program officers, CDC enhances campaign planning, monitoring, and data analysis. CDC also provides technical support for the introduction of the rotavirus vaccine and promotes the Second Year of Life (2YL) policy to improve measles immunity and sustain high vaccination coverage. One Health and Zoonotic Disease Control In coordination with the Ministries of Health, Livestock, and Environment, CDC supports Guinea’s One Health platform, which integrates human, animal, and environmental health systems to better prevent and control zoonotic diseases. The program emphasizes collaborative surveillance, policy development, and community engagement. In 2023, CDC and partners helped vaccinate dogs through a nationwide rabies control campaign and continue to support risk communication and behavioral change strategies in communities. Cross-Border Health Security CDC provides technical assistance to enhance regional health security through community-based surveillance, joint outbreak investigations, and coordinated response at key points of entry. These efforts strengthen cross-border data sharing and align Guinea’s preparedness with International Health Regulations. Fact sheet Guinea Fact Sheet Download U.S. CDC's country fact sheet for Guinea Mar 19, 2026 Download Download Success story spotlight Guinea Strengthens Laboratory Leadership Through Regional Collaboration CDC Guinea's laboratory specialists participated in the final evaluation and graduation of the Global Laboratory Leadership Program (GLLP) second cohort. As Guinea continues to respond to reoccurring public health threats such as monkeypox, Lassa fever and whopping cough, the need to strengthen laboratory leadership has become critical to improving national health security. Despite progress in diagnostics and surveillance, gaps in workforce capacity, quality management, and coordination have limited the effectiveness of the laboratory system. To address these challenges, CDC Guinea partnered with regional institutions to implement the Global Laboratory Leadership Program (GLLP), enrolling four Guinean professionals in a specialized university diploma program in Burkina Faso. In February 2026, laboratory professionals and partners gathered at Joseph Ki-Zerbo University in Ouagadougou to celebrate the GLLP graduates. CDC Guinea's laboratory specialists participated in the final evaluation and graduation of the program's second cohort—creating an opportunity to exchange knowledge and bring proven solutions back home. The results were impressive. Of 34 participants, 33 successfully graduated—a 97 percent success rate—and all four Guinean candidates passed their final presentations and evaluations, achieving a 100 percent success rate. Their projects demonstrated practical solutions to strengthen laboratory systems, improve quality, and enhance leadership skills across sectors. Beyond supporting the graduation of four Guinean laboratory professionals, the visit to Burkina Faso provided CDC Guinea with valuable lessons to strengthen laboratory systems in Guinea. Through meetings with academic institutions, laboratory leaders, and implementing partners, representatives from Guinea learned practical ways to implement GLLP, build sustainable mentorship programs, and coordinate laboratory networks. The visit also showcased examples of successful laboratory systems that could be adopted for use in Guinea. Lessons learned from the visit also showed laboratorians from Guinea how to strengthen their emergency response systems through implementing innovative approaches such as the 7-1-7 framework which improves the speed of outbreak detection and response. Building on these lessons, Guinea can now apply best practices to strengthen public health systems across the country. With continued collaboration between CDC Guinea, CDC Burkina Faso, and partners, Guinea is building a skilled laboratory workforce and a more resilient health system—better prepared to detect, respond to, and contain public health threats at their source—preventing outbreaks from spreading to neighboring communities including the U.S. Success stories Inside CDC's Guinea Monkeypox Response In June 2025, CDC and Guinea contained monkeypox through rapid detection, response, and training. Meet the world's 7 deadliest bats, famous for carrying lethal diseases "It can carry Ebola, a nasty virus that causes bleeding from every orifice and is usually fatal." Meet the world's 7 deadliest bats, famous for carrying lethal diseases Bats may be tiny and only come out at night but as carriers of some of the world’s most life-threatening viruses, one bite can pack a powerful punch Johner Images/Getty Images Cate Langmuir Published: August 14, 2026 at 3:06 am Bats play a vital role in ecosystems, from agricultural land to tropical rainforests, scooping up mosquitoes and beetles, pollinating plants and dispersing seeds. Top 10 Deadliest Insects: Tiny Killers Revealed Explore the world's most dangerous insects, from disease spreaders to venomous stingers. 0 seconds of 1 minute, 48 secondsVolume 0% Press shift question mark to access a list of keyboard shortcuts Keyboard ShortcutsEnabledDisabled Shortcuts Open/Close/ or ? Play/PauseSPACE Increase Volume↑ Decrease Volume↓ Seek Forward→ Seek Backward← Captions On/Offc Fullscreen/Exit Fullscreenf Mute/Unmutem Decrease Caption Size- Increase Caption Size+ or = Seek %0-9 Live 00:00 01:48 01:48 More Videos 01:48 Top 10 Deadliest Insects: Tiny Killers Revealed 01:46 Top 10 Deadliest Plants on Earth 01:48 Top 10 Deadliest Animals to Humans Explained 00:58 Top 10 Deadliest Sea Creatures Revealed 00:59 10 Greatest Wildlife Spectacles on Earth 00:58 Top Arctic Animals: Wildlife of the Frozen North Close But these diminutive mammals are also long-term hosts for serious viruses, including Ebola, a ferocious disease that drains its victims of bodily fluids, rabies, a disease that affects the nervous system, and, most likely, viral ancestors of Covid-19. Some of these viruses can be passed to humans and many can kill. Bats guide: species facts, what they eat, and whether they really are as blind as a - well - bat World's 10 deadliest diseases humans can get from animals – including the torturous. sleeping sickness, which affects the brain causing insomnia and worse Here’s our roundup of bats with lethal bites. Deadliest bats Vampire bat, Desmodontinae Nicolas Reusens/Getty Images The vampire bat, found in Mexico and Central and South America, famously drinks the blood of other animals to survive. They use echolocation to search for prey after dark – usually cows, pigs, horses and birds. Once a victim is located, the bat employs heat sensors in its super-powered nose to guide it to the warmest patches of skin where the blood is nearest the surface. 6 grotesque and weird vampire animals – from a creature that drinks the blood of its children to a cloaked deep-sea beast that can turn itself inside out 6 amazing blood-sucking animals that aren't insects - including a fish that's reported to have swam up a man's penis It then pierces the skin with its razor-sharp teeth before the feast begins. Each bat can lap up more than 50% of its own body weight every night, and often these light, graceful creatures can graze for more than 30 minutes without waking the animal. Unlike other species of bat, vampire bats can walk, run and hop on all fours, which helps them attach to their prey and take off after a feed. Could rabies have entered Britain? Rabies-causing virus found in Isle of Wight animal While vampire bats don’t hurt their prey with the actual bite, they do carry rabies, spread through the saliva, causing thousands of livestock deaths and a handful of human cases every year. If a human is bitten by a vampire bat, the chance of contracting rabies is much higher than the incidence rate after being bitten by a cat or dog. Big brown bat, Eptesicus fuscus JasonOndreicka/Getty Images This insect-eating species, larger than the average bat, is usually seen as an ally of the farmer as they chomp their way through vast quantities of crop-destroying insects, particularly small beetles. It’s found on the American continent, from northern Canada to the northern South America. However, a big proportion of them are reservoirs for a large number of viruses, most notably rabies, which can be transmitted to humans. Moreover, loss of habitat through deforestation is forcing their colonies into man-made structures, close to human habitats, increasing the risk of zoonotic transmission. Weird flying animals: discover the different species that can take to the sky Golden bats, boa snakes and dwarf porcupines are hiding deep inside in Mexico's ancient temples – and scientists know why Grey-headed flying fox, Pteropus poliocephalus Jamie Lamb/Getty Images Named for its fox-like head, and with a wingspan of up to a metre, this is the largest bat in Australia. Its diet consists of fruit, particularly figs, pollen and nectar of native trees, especially gum trees, making this bat a key pollinator and seed disperser. Flying foxes: These extraordinary tropical flying mammals can travel 30km a night in search of food But suffer a bite or a scratch and you could be infected with Australian bat lyssavirus (ABLV), a close relative of the rabies virus and a rare but often fatal viral disease affecting the central nervous system. Grey-headed flying foxes also carry the Hendra virus (HeV), which mostly infects horses but can spill over from horses into humans. It's wider than a doorway, bigger than a buzzard yet weighs less than a suitcase... In South and South East Asia, the Malaysian flying fox is a natural host for Nipah, a virus that causes inflammation of the brain and which has a high mortality rate. While it can arise through direct contact with an infected animal, many infections result from the consumption of fruit products contaminated with the poo, urine or saliva of infected bats. Egyptian tomb bat, Taphozous perforatus Used under Creative Commons via Wikipedia, credit: Description de l'Égypte The first specimen of this bat to be collected was from a royal tomb in Egypt, in 1818 – hence the name. It’s a medium-sized insectivore native to parts of Africa, the Arabian peninsula and India and roosts in old buildings, tunnels or wells, in colonies of up to several thousand. It might not have any ears, but that doesn't stop it having the best hearing in the animal kingdom. Here's why... It was identified as a likely carrier of the coronavirus responsible for the deadly 2013 MERS (Middle East Respiratory Syndrome) outbreak in Saudi Arabia, though scientists believe the transmission was through contact with camels, rather than directly from the bats. Free-tailed bat, Molossidae Poetra RH/Getty Images This describes any of 100 species of bats, so-called for the way in which part of the tail extends beyond the membrane connecting the hind legs. Also known as the wrinkle-lipped bat for their heavy snouts, their distribution is in tropical and subtropical regions. With a population of 15 million this is the biggest mammal gathering on Earth – and it happens in Texas... With speeds of 100 miles per hour, it leaves birds like swifts and albatrosses eating its dust. They are gregarious animals and often live in large groups in caves, tree holes and even buildings – some colonies number in the millions, such as the Mexican free-tailed bat. They mainly feed on insects like moths and beetles, making them an important pest predator in nature. But some species of this bat can carry Ebola, a nasty virus that causes bleeding from every orifice and is usually fatal. According to research, the Angolan free-tailed bat may have been the carrier responsible for the catastrophic West African Ebola epidemic that killed more than 11,000 people between 2013-2016. More recently, researchers have identified a potential pandemic threat, in the shape of the Bombali ebolavirus in Angolan and little free-tailed bats in Sierra Leone, and later in Kenya. Egyptian fruit bat, Rousettus aegyptiacus Collinswood Images/Getty Images The fruit-eating bat is found throughout Africa and the Middle East, and as far as Pakistan and northern India. It lives in colonies of several thousand, usually caves near forests with ample fruit production, of which it is a voracious consumer – they can consume 50-150% of their body weight in fruit each night. Most of the day is spent sleeping or grooming. World's biggest animal migration is an aerial spectacle worthy of a place on Africa's Big 6, says Mike Dilger Camera traps film predators descending on cave filled with 40,000 bats. What happens next is staggering Unfortunately, these bats are also natural hosts for Marburg virus disease (MVD), a close cousin of Ebola. Formerly known as Marburg haemorrhagic fever, it’s a severe illness in humans with an average fatality of 50%. Living viruses were found in bats in a cave in Uganda after miners working there were infected. In 2024, Rwanda reported the country’s first outbreak and Tanzania declared another outbreak in 2025. Horseshoe bat, Rhinolophidae mauribo/Getty Images This strange-looking bat (in the family Rhinolophidae) is named for the horseshoe-shaped fleshy protuberance on its nose, which is thought to help it focus its echolocation calls while hunting. There are more than 100 species of horseshoe bat and they are mainly found in tropical and temperate regions, from Europe and Japan and from Asia to Africa, where they prey on insects, such as flies, moths and beetles. Horseshoe bats guide: how to identify, where they live, and how they are making a comeback "Vision and echolocation are less useful on long migration routes..." So how do bats navigate? This bat could be classed as one of the world’s most dangerous because it is widely considered to be a natural reservoir and source of zoonotic coronaviruses (CoVs), some of which, as we now know only too well, can cause highly contagious respiratory diseases in humans. Strong similarities between some coronavirus genomes in horseshoe bats and those of SARS-CoV (the virus responsible for the 2002 SARS outbreak) and SARS-CoV-2 (the virus responsible for COVID-19) suggest that these coronaviruses may have first emerged in horseshoe bats before mutating and jumping species, either directly or through an intermediary animal species to humans. . Meet the world's 7 deadliest bats, famous for carrying lethal diseases Bats may be tiny and only come out at night but as carriers of some of the world’s most life-threatening viruses, one bite can pack a powerful punch Johner Images/Getty Images Cate Langmuir Published: August 14, 2026 at 3:06 am Bats play a vital role in ecosystems, from agricultural land to tropical rainforests, scooping up mosquitoes and beetles, pollinating plants and dispersing seeds. Play/PauseSPACE Increase Volume↑ Decrease Volume↓ Seek Forward→ Seek Backward← Captions On/Offc Fullscreen/Exit Fullscreenf Mute/Unmutem Decrease Caption Size- Increase Caption Size+ or = Seek %0-9 Live 00:00 01:48 01:48 More Videos 01:48 Top 10 Deadliest Insects: Tiny Killers Revealed 01:46 Top 10 Deadliest Plants on Earth 01:48 Top 10 Deadliest Animals to Humans Explained 00:58 Top 10 Deadliest Sea Creatures Revealed 00:59 10 Greatest Wildlife Spectacles on Earth 00:58 Top Arctic Animals: Wildlife of the Frozen North Close But these diminutive mammals are also long-term hosts for serious viruses, including Ebola, a ferocious disease that drains its victims of bodily fluids, rabies, a disease that affects the nervous system, and, most likely, viral ancestors of Covid-19. Some of these viruses can be passed to humans and many can kill. Bats guide: species facts, what they eat, and whether they really are as blind as a - well - bat World's 10 deadliest diseases humans can get from animals – including the torturous. sleeping sickness, which affects the brain causing insomnia and worse Here’s our roundup of bats with lethal bites. Deadliest bats Vampire bat, Desmodontinae Nicolas Reusens/Getty Images The vampire bat, found in Mexico and Central and South America, famously drinks the blood of other animals to survive. They use echolocation to search for prey after dark – usually cows, pigs, horses and birds. Once a victim is located, the bat employs heat sensors in its super-powered nose to guide it to the warmest patches of skin where the blood is nearest the surface. 6 grotesque and weird vampire animals – from a creature that drinks the blood of its children to a cloaked deep-sea beast that can turn itself inside out 6 amazing blood-sucking animals that aren't insects - including a fish that's reported to have swam up a man's penis It then pierces the skin with its razor-sharp teeth before the feast begins. Each bat can lap up more than 50% of its own body weight every night, and often these light, graceful creatures can graze for more than 30 minutes without waking the animal. Unlike other species of bat, vampire bats can walk, run and hop on all fours, which helps them attach to their prey and take off after a feed. Could rabies have entered Britain? Rabies-causing virus found in Isle of Wight animal While vampire bats don’t hurt their prey with the actual bite, they do carry rabies, spread through the saliva, causing thousands of livestock deaths and a handful of human cases every year. If a human is bitten by a vampire bat, the chance of contracting rabies is much higher than the incidence rate after being bitten by a cat or dog. Big brown bat, Eptesicus fuscus JasonOndreicka/Getty Images This insect-eating species, larger than the average bat, is usually seen as an ally of the farmer as they chomp their way through vast quantities of crop-destroying insects, particularly small beetles. It’s found on the American continent, from northern Canada to the northern South America. However, a big proportion of them are reservoirs for a large number of viruses, most notably rabies, which can be transmitted to humans. Moreover, loss of habitat through deforestation is forcing their colonies into man-made structures, close to human habitats, increasing the risk of zoonotic transmission. Weird flying animals: discover the different species that can take to the sky Golden bats, boa snakes and dwarf porcupines are hiding deep inside in Mexico's ancient temples – and scientists know why Grey-headed flying fox, Pteropus poliocephalus Jamie Lamb/Getty Images Named for its fox-like head, and with a wingspan of up to a metre, this is the largest bat in Australia. Its diet consists of fruit, particularly figs, pollen and nectar of native trees, especially gum trees, making this bat a key pollinator and seed disperser. Flying foxes: These extraordinary tropical flying mammals can travel 30km a night in search of food But suffer a bite or a scratch and you could be infected with Australian bat lyssavirus (ABLV), a close relative of the rabies virus and a rare but often fatal viral disease affecting the central nervous system. Grey-headed flying foxes also carry the Hendra virus (HeV), which mostly infects horses but can spill over from horses into humans. It's wider than a doorway, bigger than a buzzard yet weighs less than a suitcase... In South and South East Asia, the Malaysian flying fox is a natural host for Nipah, a virus that causes inflammation of the brain and which has a high mortality rate. While it can arise through direct contact with an infected animal, many infections result from the consumption of fruit products contaminated with the poo, urine or saliva of infected bats. Egyptian tomb bat, Taphozous perforatus Used under Creative Commons via Wikipedia, credit: Description de l'Égypte The first specimen of this bat to be collected was from a royal tomb in Egypt, in 1818 – hence the name. It’s a medium-sized insectivore native to parts of Africa, the Arabian peninsula and India and roosts in old buildings, tunnels or wells, in colonies of up to several thousand. It might not have any ears, but that doesn't stop it having the best hearing in the animal kingdom. Here's why... It was identified as a likely carrier of the coronavirus responsible for the deadly 2013 MERS (Middle East Respiratory Syndrome) outbreak in Saudi Arabia, though scientists believe the transmission was through contact with camels, rather than directly from the bats. Free-tailed bat, Molossidae Poetra RH/Getty Images This describes any of 100 species of bats, so-called for the way in which part of the tail extends beyond the membrane connecting the hind legs. Also known as the wrinkle-lipped bat for their heavy snouts, their distribution is in tropical and subtropical regions. With a population of 15 million this is the biggest mammal gathering on Earth – and it happens in Texas... With speeds of 100 miles per hour, it leaves birds like swifts and albatrosses eating its dust. They are gregarious animals and often live in large groups in caves, tree holes and even buildings – some colonies number in the millions, such as the Mexican free-tailed bat. They mainly feed on insects like moths and beetles, making them an important pest predator in nature. But some species of this bat can carry Ebola, a nasty virus that causes bleeding from every orifice and is usually fatal. According to research, the Angolan free-tailed bat may have been the carrier responsible for the catastrophic West African Ebola epidemic that killed more than 11,000 people between 2013-2016. More recently, researchers have identified a potential pandemic threat, in the shape of the Bombali ebolavirus in Angolan and little free-tailed bats in Sierra Leone, and later in Kenya. Egyptian fruit bat, Rousettus aegyptiacus Collinswood Images/Getty Images The fruit-eating bat is found throughout Africa and the Middle East, and as far as Pakistan and northern India. It lives in colonies of several thousand, usually caves near forests with ample fruit production, of which it is a voracious consumer – they can consume 50-150% of their body weight in fruit each night. Most of the day is spent sleeping or grooming. World's biggest animal migration is an aerial spectacle worthy of a place on Africa's Big 6, says Mike Dilger Camera traps film predators descending on cave filled with 40,000 bats. What happens next is staggering Unfortunately, these bats are also natural hosts for Marburg virus disease (MVD), a close cousin of Ebola. Formerly known as Marburg haemorrhagic fever, it’s a severe illness in humans with an average fatality of 50%. Living viruses were found in bats in a cave in Uganda after miners working there were infected. In 2024, Rwanda reported the country’s first outbreak and Tanzania declared another outbreak in 2025. Horseshoe bat, Rhinolophidae mauribo/Getty Images This strange-looking bat (in the family Rhinolophidae) is named for the horseshoe-shaped fleshy protuberance on its nose, which is thought to help it focus its echolocation calls while hunting. There are more than 100 species of horseshoe bat and they are mainly found in tropical and temperate regions, from Europe and Japan and from Asia to Africa, where they prey on insects, such as flies, moths and beetles. Horseshoe bats guide: how to identify, where they live, and how they are making a comeback "Vision and echolocation are less useful on long migration routes..." So how do bats navigate? This bat could be classed as one of the world’s most dangerous because it is widely considered to be a natural reservoir and source of zoonotic coronaviruses (CoVs), some of which, as we now know only too well, can cause highly contagious respiratory diseases in humans. Strong similarities between some coronavirus genomes in horseshoe bats and those of SARS-CoV (the virus responsible for the 2002 SARS outbreak) and SARS-CoV-2 (the virus responsible for COVID-19) suggest that these coronaviruses may have first emerged in horseshoe bats before mutating and jumping species, either directly or through an intermediary animal species to humans. .
